title: Toronto shooting reopens debate over police handling of mentally ill suspects
article: Friday's fatal shooting by Toronto police of 30-year-old Devon LaFleur has again raised questions about how police handle confrontations with the mentally ill.
And why, asks leading forensic psychiatrist John Bradford, are police officers increasingly called upon to be on the front lines of a nationwide mental-health problem?
According to relatives, the Ottawa man had struggled for much of his life with bipolar disorder. He went missing on Friday and was shot to death that night outside a North York women's shelter.
LaFleur's family said he was in Toronto to visit a woman at the shelter but before leaving Ottawa to see his friend had allegedly robbed a Kanata bank at gunpoint.

LaFleur's father apparently alerted Ottawa police that his son had left for Toronto and might have been carrying an air pistol.
It remains unclear how the confrontation that led several officers to open fire on LaFleur developed or whether he was brandishing a weapon.
The provincial Special Investigation Unit (SIU) is investigating.
Given the number of interactions between police and the mentally ill, experts say that fatal incidents are relatively uncommon.
Royal hospital doctor Bradford was part of a team of experts asked to examine Toronto police interaction with "persons in crisis" after the 2013 police shooting of teenager Sammy Yatim.

Toronto police have more than 20,000 incidents involving the mentally ill every year and according to Bradford, the number is rising and currently includes about 12,000 emergency cases where people often need immediate hospitalization.
"They are probably doing a pretty good job," said Bradford, "but the real question is why are police on the front lines of the mental health crisis in their community?

"Over the years, mental health has been underfunded and hospital beds closed," he added. "There was a theory that community resources would fill the gap but that never happened so you have homeless, mentally ill people getting into difficulties in every city of this country.
"They become increasingly criminalized so you have more people in jail with mental disorder and in most instances they get sub-adequate treatment," he said.

Before taking "lethal force" and shooting a suspect in the torso, Toronto police are typically required to try non-lethal force first - firing the Taser and the "bean bag" which is a projectile intended to wind and temporarily incapacitates a suspect.

"I don't know whether that happened in this case but it was part of our recommendations," said Bradford. "If there's a gun - whether they know if it's an air pistol or not - they might go to lethal force more rapidly.
"The sad part is that this was a mentally ill person living in the community and not criminally responsible," he added.

Dr. Peter Boyles, an emergency psychiatrist at The Ottawa Hospital's Civic campus led a program with Ottawa police where psychiatrists and trainee psychiatrists travelled with officers responding to incidents involving mentally ill suspects.
With access to mental health records, the doctors were able to advise officers on how best to approach specific suspects.
Boyles resigned from the program last June but continues holding occasional two-day workshops for officers interested in learning how to interact with the mentally ill.

"On a day-to-day basis the police do an excellent job in dealing with the vast majority of mentally ill cases," said Boyles. "I work in the emergency and every day, police are appropriately bringing in mentally ill people and are treating them with utmost respect.

"But police do a much better job of dealing with someone when they have information," he added. "One problem is that they arrive at these scenes not knowing if a person is mentally ill and if they are, how do they usually behave? So they are dealing with the situation blind."
Lack of communication between police and mental health professionals remains a problem, said Boyles.

"Police have their information and hospitals and mental health professionals have their information but they don't communicate," he said. "And that communication was what was most effective in our program."

(Ottawa police say the force's relationship with the hospital continues but Boyles says it is now an 'after the fact' program involving social workers and no longer includes mental health professionals providing officers with real time information).
It's too early to assess what happened in the LaFleur case, added Boyles.

"We don't have all the information from Toronto but my questions would be: 'Were the police well equipped with the information they needed and what sort of skill sets did they have to defuse the situation?'"
